transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corova Coleman.
The U.S. and Israel are preparing plans for a possible attack on Iran in early November after the midterm elections.
That's according to a person briefed on the matter speaking to NPR.
From Tel Aviv, NPR's Daniel Estrin reports.
The person briefed on the U.S. and Israel's war planning spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity to discuss the preparations.
The person said Israel had initially planned to strike Iran in mid-October about two weeks before Israeli elections October 27, but President Trump objected.
The person briefed said the U.S. is now amassing forces in the region to be ready for an attack by early November after U.S. midterms November 3,
but that these preparations could also be part of a campaign to pressure Iran to reach a diplomatic deal.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is campaigning for re-election on a threat to topple Iran's regime.
Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
Stocks fell this morning with the tech-heavy NASDAQ down sharply.
Continued tensions in the Middle East have sparked a global sell-off and led to higher oil prices.
NPR's Rafael Naam has the story.
The unresolved tensions with Iran and the escalating attacks by Houthi militants in Saudi Arabia are keeping investors on edge.
Brent crude, the global benchmark, gained sharply, while stock markets from Tokyo to Hong Kong declined overnight.
In the U.S., another factor is the tumble in A.I. stocks such as Nvidia amid continued concerns about the huge spending being done by companies across the sector.
U.S. bond markets, though, which had taken a hit earlier this year, are rising as investors are opting for an investment that has traditionally been seen as safer.
Rafael Naam, NPR News.
President Trump made gains with young voters in 2024.
But two years later, more than six in ten Gen Z voters say their midterm vote this fall is in opposition to the president and his policies.
That's according to a new Harvard youth poll released today.
It surveyed more than 2,000 voters between the ages of 18 and 29.
NPR's Alina Moore has more.
Democrats have a big advantage in the latest Harvard youth poll.
Among Gen Zers who say they're definitely voting this fall, 63 percent plan to vote for Democrats,
compared to just a quarter-voting Republican and one in ten who are undecided.
There's also an enthusiasm gap, with more young Democrats than young Republicans saying they're definitely going to vote.
But overall, only one-third of Gen Z plans to vote, which is down from 40 percent ahead of the 2018 and 2022 midterms.
What's more, most young people will remain unhappy with the state of the country,
with just nine percent saying they feel the country is headed in the right direction, a record low for the poll.
Alina Moore, NPR News.
On Wall Street, the Dow was down 75 points.
The Nasdaq is down 400.
This is NPR.
President Trump flies to Iowa today to campaign for Republican candidates.
He will visit Sioux City.
Vice President Vance will campaign today in central Nebraska.
A federal judge in California is restricting the Department of Homeland Security's field operations in nine states.
That's where DHS is targeting non-citizens who previously voted.
As NPR's Jude Joffee Block reports, the ruling cites the Voting Rights Act, which bars voter intimidation.
The Trump administration has been laser-focused on finding and arresting non-citizens who illegally voted.
Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin wrote that effort is using data that appears unreliable.
And she wrote federal officers knocking on doors looking for people based on that data is intimidating eligible voters.
She also noted federal officials are targeting new citizens who may have voted before naturalizing.
The order blocks federal officers from targeting people known or suspected to be U.S. citizens or relying on incomplete data without further investigation.
The order is set to take effect Friday and stay in place through election night, though the federal government could appeal.
Jude Joffee Block, NPR News.
The National Hurricane Center, says subtropical storm Josephine, is still bringing significant coastal flooding to parts of the eastern seaboard.
Forecasters say Josephine's top sustained winds are about 65 miles per hour and it's nearly 200 miles southeast of Nantucket, Massachusetts.
The storm should move away from the U.S. and stay south of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland in the next couple of days.
This is NPR.

topics.text: U.S. and Israel plan possible Iran attack in early November after midterm elections
Global stocks fall and oil prices rise amid Middle East tensions and AI stock sell-off
Harvard youth poll finds most Gen Z voters oppose Trump and his policies ahead of midterms
Trump to campaign in Iowa and Vance in Nebraska ahead of midterm elections
Federal judge in California restricts DHS field operations targeting non-citizen voters in nine states
Subtropical Storm Josephine brings coastal flooding to Eastern Seaboard, moving away from U.S.
